title: Famine warning across Darfur and Kordofan
deck: A UN-backed famine alert says war, displacement and El Niño drought are pushing Sudan's west and south toward famine, just as the aid appeal is more than half unfunded and convoys are coming under fire.
region: Sudan (Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan); Horn of Africa

card.headline: Sudan's war and drought are pushing Darfur and Kordofan toward famine, and the money to respond is not there

keyNumber.label: of children acutely malnourished in one South Darfur camp (30.8% in another); the famine-area threshold is 30%

forYou.line: Sudan sits in the Cairo-Khartoum-Mogadishu bloc facing Addis Ababa, so the famine and the Ethiopia-Eritrea crisis may interact.

whatHappened: On 12 October 2026 the IPC issued an alert: war, displacement and El Niño drought are speeding up the risk of famine across Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Its Famine Review Committee said there was not enough survey data for a full analysis, but the evidence points to a rapidly worsening situation.

Its headline numbers: acute malnutrition among children of 38% and 30.8% in two South Darfur camps, both above the 30% famine threshold. Drought affects more than half of the country, and about half of its cropland shows poor plant growth (64% in North Darfur). 8.58 million internally people are displaced nationwide, and over 300,000 have fled Kordofan since October 2025.
Aid is not keeping up. As of 8 October, the 2026 humanitarian plan was 57% unfunded. WFP-contracted convoys came under fire on 2 and 3 October. The sources we used do not say who fired.
whyItMatters: Famine is the most severe food-insecurity classification. A warning at this scale in a country already at war means very high risks of child deaths if aid does not scale up. The IPC's formal famine label also needs mortality and food-access evidence, not malnutrition alone, so an alert is not the same as a declaration.
The causes reinforce each other. War displaces farmers and blocks roads. Drought shrinks harvests. Underfunding shrinks the response. Each makes the others worse.

The crisis reaches beyond Sudan. Brent above $100 and Red Sea disruption from the Gulf war make fuel and food aid dearer to ship to Port Sudan. In our judgement, funding gaps like Sudan's are likely to feature in arguments over the EU's 2028-2034 external-aid envelope. Sudan is part of the Cairo-Khartoum-Mogadishu bloc facing Addis Ababa, so the Ethiopia-Eritrea crisis is not a separate story.

winners.why: Famine is a loss for nearly everyone. Armed groups that control access may gain leverage over civilians and aid, but that is an analytical judgement, not a reported fact.

winners.who: Advocates of larger aid and external-action budgets
winners.why: The alert strengthens the case for a bigger EU external-aid envelope in the 2028-2034 talks (our judgement).

losers.who: Children and families in South Darfur camps
losers.why: Malnutrition rates above the famine threshold are the most direct measure of harm in the alert.

losers.who: Displaced people in Darfur and Kordofan
losers.why: 8.58 million are displaced nationally; over 300,000 have fled Kordofan since October 2025.
About half of Sudan's cropland shows poor plant growth in the drought, which threatens both food and income.
They face a 57% funding gap and fire on WFP-contracted convoys on 2 and 3 October.

whatsNext: Possible further IPC analysis and formal classification of specific areas, if data can be collected. The alert does not say when.
Pressure on donors to close the 57% gap. Watch for new pledges or ration-cut announcements by agencies.
The EU aims to agree its 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026, with the external-aid envelope part of the argument.
Access incidents. Further attacks on convoys would show whether aid can reach Darfur and Kordofan at all.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path over the next six months?
options: A rapid aid scale-up closes the funding gap and averts famine
Alerts continue while aid remains underfunded and access stays contested
The war ends and aid flows freely
Famine is formally confirmed in many new areas at once
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 40%, is that more areas are formally classified in famine or near it while funding stays well short and access stays contested. The slow-grind case is next at about 35%. Probabilities are our judgement, not a sourced forecast.

causes.name: Prolonged war
causes.detail: Fighting since April 2023 has displaced millions and disrupted farming, markets and roads.

causes.name: Fragile food system
causes.detail: Sudan depends on rain-fed farming and on trade routes that fighting keeps cutting (general knowledge, not in the sources).

causes.name: Chronic aid dependence
causes.detail: With 8.58 million people displaced, much of the population relies on humanitarian deliveries that are now underfunded.

causes.name: Kordofan displacement

causes.name: Camp malnutrition crossing the threshold

stakeholders.wants: Action before deaths rise, backed by credible data
stakeholders.leverage: Its classifications shape donor and UN decisions
stakeholders.likelyMove: Follow up with further analysis as data allows; the sources give no dates

stakeholders.name: WFP and UN agencies
stakeholders.wants: Safe access and funding for the 2026 plan
stakeholders.likelyMove: Press donors and parties for access; prioritise the most severe areas (estimate)

stakeholders.name: Sudan's army and its civilian authorities
stakeholders.role: Parties to the war; the army-aligned government announced its return from Port Sudan to Khartoum in January 2026
stakeholders.wants: Military and political advantage; control over aid access
stakeholders.likelyMove: Not stated in the sources; we judge that access disputes will continue

stakeholders.name: Rapid Support Forces and other armed groups
stakeholders.role: Parties to the war in Darfur and Kordofan
stakeholders.leverage: Control of roads and areas where aid must pass
stakeholders.likelyMove: Not stated in the sources; the alert notes that fighting and displacement continue

stakeholders.role: Providers of the funding behind the plan
stakeholders.leverage: Money, and in the EU's case the 2028-2034 budget envelope
stakeholders.likelyMove: Mixed: appeals for more, but budgets under pressure from other crises (judgement)

stakeholders.likelyMove: Continue positioning over the Ethiopia-Eritrea crisis; effects on Sudan's aid routes are uncertain

sectors.why: About half of cropland shows poor plant growth in the drought, and displacement removes farmers from the land.
Convoys were fired on 2 and 3 October and freight and fuel costs remain high.
Child acute malnutrition above 30% in two camps signals services that are overstretched.

sectors.sector: Red Sea and Port Sudan shipping
sectors.why: Red Sea disruption and Brent above $100 raise the cost of reaching Port Sudan.
The 57% gap strengthens calls for more aid, but leaders face tight budgets and elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Scarcity in Sudan may lift prices at the borders; the size of the effect is not in the sources (estimate).

dailyLife.effect: For families in the affected areas, drought and displacement reduce what can be grown and bought; child acute malnutrition is at 38% and 30.8% in two South Darfur camps.
With the plan 57% unfunded, agencies may have to cut or narrow rations. This is our estimate, not a reported decision.
Fire on WFP-contracted convoys on 2 and 3 October shows how risky roads are for both aid workers and civilians.
The same Gulf war that raises aid-shipping costs also pushed French diesel to a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.
For readers in the EU, the argument over how much to spend on external aid in 2028-2034 is a question of how much of the common budget goes to crises like this.

scenarios.name: More famine classifications
scenarios.looksLike: Further IPC analysis confirms famine or famine-like conditions in more localities of Darfur and Kordofan as the lean period bites; the funding gap stays above 40%.
signposts: New IPC or FRC analysis with famine classifications
Reports of rising child deaths from agencies
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Louder donor appeals, more pressure on the EU external-aid budget, and more displacement toward camps and borders.

scenarios.name: Slow grind
scenarios.looksLike: Alerts continue, aid is partial, access is contested, and agencies prioritise the worst areas without a breakthrough.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A chronic emergency that keeps displacing people and draws steady but insufficient attention.

scenarios.name: Regional spillover
scenarios.looksLike: Escalation in the Ethiopia-Eritrea crisis and Red Sea tension disrupt aid corridors or draw in the Cairo-Khartoum-Mogadishu bloc more directly, and displacement crosses borders.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A wider Horn of Africa crisis that competes for aid and attention.

scenarios.name: Access and funding breakthrough
scenarios.looksLike: A humanitarian pause or new corridors combine with a large donor top-up that cuts the funding gap sharply.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Famine risk eases in the most exposed areas, though the underlying war and drought remain.

predictions.text: About 65%: the IPC or its Famine Review Committee will classify at least one additional locality in Darfur or Kordofan as in famine or famine-like conditions.
About 85%: Sudan's 2026 humanitarian plan will still be more than 40% unfunded at year-end.
About 60%: at least one more attack on or serious obstruction of a WFP or UN aid convoy in Sudan will be publicly reported.
About 45%: EU leaders will not agree the 2028-2034 budget by the end-2026 target.
About 25%: a formal humanitarian pause or access agreement for Darfur or Kordofan will be announced.

actions: Review exposure to Port Sudan, Red Sea routes and Sudan's neighbours; add buffers and force-majeure clauses.
Plan for higher fuel and freight costs while Brent stays above $100.
If you operate in the region, update staff safety plans given fire on convoys on 2 and 3 October.
Treat Sudan and the wider Horn of Africa as a cluster of linked risks, including the Ethiopia-Eritrea crisis.
Watch Red Sea shipping and oil prices for contagion to freight costs.
Track the EU 2028-2034 budget outcome for aid-related spending.
If you donate, consider established humanitarian groups working in Sudan, and check how they handle access and security.
Expect fuel and food prices to stay elevated while the Gulf war continues.
Close the 57% funding gap with front-loaded money rather than late pledges.
Press all parties for safe, predictable convoy access and investigate attacks on aid.
Ring-fence external aid in the 2028-2034 budget negotiations rather than trading it away.
Coordinate Sudan and Tigray appeals so that donors do not treat them as rivals.

analogues.whatFollowed: General knowledge: early warnings preceded a famine in which many people died; the delay in response became a lesson for donors on acting early.
General knowledge, medium confidence: famine was confirmed in a Darfur camp during this same war; response remained limited by access and funding.
General knowledge: war, access limits and hunger combined; this shows how conflict blocks aid even when need is well documented.

evidence.method: Drafted from the two listed sources (UN News and Sudan Tribune), the matched headlines and the event summary, plus three connected events (Ethiopia-Eritrea, the Gulf energy shock and the EU 2028-2034 budget) already judged elsewhere. I could not read the full IPC alert, so the figures are as summarised in the event record. Background on the war, the 2024 famine finding and IPC thresholds comes from general knowledge and is flagged as medium confidence. Effects on aid rations, disease, prices and displacement, along with scenario probabilities and predictions, are estimates by the author.
